title: Conflict check delays new client intake on Mac: causes and fixes for lawyers in 2026
metaTitle: Conflict check delays new client intake: causes and fixes
description: Conflict checks slow new client intake because they rely on memory and loose lists. Here is what that costs and the fixes you can use this week.
targetKeyword: conflict check delays new client intake
intro: Conflict check delays slow new client intake when the check is manual, late, or spread across several places. Most small firms run it from memory, a paper form, or a plain list, so every prospect adds search time. This page covers why it happens, what it costs, and fixes you can use without buying anything.
tldr: Conflict checks slow intake when they depend on memory, paper forms, or a plain email search.
Name variants and unrecorded related parties are the usual reasons a check misses a conflict.
Free fixes: collect every name at intake, search the variants, and re-run the check when parties change.
Stop collecting details once you can decline, and warn the prospect that you have not agreed to act.

blocks.text: A conflict check asks one question. Has this firm already worked for, against, or alongside this person or company? At intake, that search has to finish before you can say yes to a consultation. When it drags on, the prospect calls the next firm. When it gets rushed, you risk a conflict you never see.
Why the check slows intake in the first place

Most delays come from three habits. The check starts late, it runs from memory, and it searches one list in one place. Each habit adds a loop. You find a possible match, pull the file, ask a partner, and wait. The prospect waits the whole time.

Here is a common pattern. A prospect calls about a boundary dispute. The caller names a neighbor, a landscaping company, and a former spouse. Your list has the spouse under one spelling and the company under an older name. The first search comes back clear. A week later a partner remembers the old company, and the check starts again from zero.
Why conflicts get missed: name variants and related parties
The NC Bar lists the usual blind spots. A check that only matches exact spelling will miss most of them. Read the list and ask which ones your intake form would catch today.

items: Maiden names, aliases, and former names
Former entity names and d/b/a names
Witnesses and the principals of a company
Related parties nobody wrote down at intake

blocks.text: How common is manual conflict checking?

Software is not universal. The ABA's 2018 Legal Technology Survey, as cited by the North Carolina Bar, found that 59% of solo practitioners had no conflict-checking software. Among lawyers in firms of 2 to 9 attorneys, 34% said they had none. No newer figure from that survey was available for this page, so treat these numbers as dated.

The NC Bar also says spreadsheets, Outlook, and Gmail are inadequate for conflict checking without significant customization. That matters if your check is a sheet of names and a search box. It works for a few matters. It breaks as the list grows and the people on it change.
What a slow conflict check costs your firm

The cost is not one number. It shows up as lost prospects, lost hours, malpractice risk, and burnout. Published figures exist for some of these and not others. Where there is no figure, this page says so.
Lost hours and admin load

In a June 2025 Rev and Centiment survey of 550 U.S. legal professionals, 49% spent seven or more hours a week on administrative or non-specialized work. Of that group, 28% spent more than 10 hours. Also, 78% said preparatory or administrative tasks kept them from essential duties. Rev ran that survey and it is not weighted, so read it as direction, not a precise count.
Malpractice exposure

Conflicts show up often in malpractice claims. Insurance Journal reported in 2018 that seven of the nine insurers surveyed by Ames and Gough cited conflicts as the first or second leading cause of claims. Insurers have named conflicts as the most common alleged error every year the survey has run. Nine insurers is a small sample, but the pattern holds.
Disqualification and firm-wide imputation

ABA Formal Opinion 510, released March 20, 2024, says that if a lawyer hears unnecessary details from a prospect, the conflict can be imputed to the whole firm. The firm must also screen the disqualified lawyer in time. A slow check makes this harder, because details often arrive before anyone knows the answer.
Burnout and staff turnover

The same Rev survey found that 79.8% of legal professionals reported burnout-related feelings in the past year. Nearly 60% had seriously considered leaving their role or the profession because of stress or burnout. Intake is one place admin piles up. Fixing the check will not fix burnout alone, but it removes a chore that repeats for every new prospect.
Mistakes people make with conflict checks
The most common mistake is checking only the person who called. The second is checking after you have already heard the case. Both are fixable, and neither needs new software.

items: Checking the caller but not the adverse party
Running the check after a long intake call
Treating a clear search as final when the facts change
Ignoring former names and d/b/a names
Letting a partner clear a name in the hallway with no record
Collecting full case details before you can decline

blocks.text: Hallway clearances are the sneakiest one. The NC Bar describes informal checks as in the moment and dependent on recall. If nobody wrote the answer down, nobody can prove it later.
Fixes you can use this week without buying anything

These fixes come from professional guidance, mainly the NC Bar best practices and ABA Formal Opinion 510. None of them needs a new vendor. They need a written routine, one shared list, and a clear point where intake stops.
Collect every name before the consultation

The NC Bar recommends gathering and checking conflict information before the initial consultation. Build an intake form with fields for the caller, the adverse party, prior names, spouses or former spouses, related companies, and witnesses. Save it as a Word template so nobody rebuilds it from memory.
Search name variants, not just exact spellings

Search each name in three forms. Use the name as given, a likely misspelling, and any former or maiden name. Write the variants into the record, so the next search finds them too. The NC Bar recommends fuzzy searching and recording prior names. If your search tool lacks fuzzy matching, run the variants by hand and log that you did.

blocks.caption: Variants to search from one intake call

blocks.text: Keep one shared list and date every check

Keep one list that everyone uses. Add a column for the date each matter was checked and the names searched. A dated log shows what was checked and when. It also tells you exactly what to re-run when a new party joins. A spreadsheet can do this, but only if someone keeps it current.
Re-run the check when the parties change

The NC Bar says to check again before providing legal services, when a new party joins, and when a lawyer with prior legal experience is hired. Set a reminder for each moment. In Apple Reminders, add a due date and put the matter name and the names to search in the note.
Stop the inquiry once you can decline

ABA Formal Opinion 510 says to warn the prospect that you have not agreed to take the matter. It also says to stop asking questions once there is a basis to decline. Say it plainly. Tell the prospect you have not agreed to represent them, and ask them to hold details until you confirm you can act.
Screen lateral hires before the offer

The ABA Journal describes conflict checks as searches of computerized lists of clients and cases, usually done before a lateral lawyer is formally hired. It cites ABA Formal Opinion 09-455 on sharing basic conflicts information with careful timing and need-to-know limits. Run the lateral's old matters before the offer goes out, not in their first week.
A worked example: one intake call, five searchable names

Take a call about a boundary dispute. The caller is named Lopez-Reyes. The adverse party is Daniel Reyes. The adverse company is Reyes Yard LLC, formerly Lopez Yard Co. A surveyor is listed as a witness. That gives you five names to search, and the table above lists the variants for each.

Search Lopez-Reyes, Lopez Reyes, and Lopez. Search Daniel Reyes and Reyes Daniel. Search Reyes Yard and Lopez Yard Co. Add the surveyor. Record each name and today's date in the shared list. Then set the re-run reminder for the day the parties change. Careful work at intake beats a missed conflict later.

blocks.title: Check your own rules first
blocks.text: Conflict and client-data rules depend on your state, your bar, and your employer. Confirm each step with your ethics counsel or bar guidance before you change how intake works.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It points at things and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons for you, and it does not connect to your conflict database. Lazur cannot run your conflict search.
Steps around the search

Lazur helps with the work around the search. It can explain a report screen, point to the prior names field, and draft the prospect warning in Outlook or Apple Mail. You can hold fn and dictate the list of related parties at the cursor. Lazur types clean text where your cursor sits. You still decide what the results mean.
Research stays in its own tabs

Lazur's research runs in its own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Use it to gather public web pages about an entity name. Check every result against its source yourself. Research does not search your firm's conflict list, so keep your official search where it is.
Keep client data inside firm rules

Lawyers, nurses, accountants, and other regulated professionals must follow employer rules on client or patient data. When you hold ⌥⌘, Lazur sends the audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. Those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Check your firm policy before you hold the shortcut over a client file.
Measure one thing for two weeks

Track the days from first call to a cleared check. Write down the date of each step in your shared list. After two weeks you have your own baseline. That beats any vendor claim, and it shows which step is slow. Most firms find the wait is in one step, not all of them.
Vendor blogs often quote minutes per check. This page leaves those out. I could not trace them to primary data. No controlled study I found shows that any tool cuts check time or errors.
Conflict check software options to review

Some firms buy software after they outgrow a shared list. Client Conflict Check describes a cloud tool that searches as you type and offers a free 30-day trial. Its homepage lists Chrome and other browsers and does not name macOS. Check their pricing page for current costs, and confirm Mac support before you sign up.

faq.question: How long does a conflict check take?
faq.answer: No primary source gives a reliable time per check for small firms. The time depends on how many names you search and how your list is kept. Track your own days from first call to cleared check for two weeks. That gives you a baseline you can trust.

faq.question: Do solo lawyers need conflict software?
faq.answer: Not always, but memory alone is risky. The NC Bar describes solo checks that rely on recall as weak. In the ABA's 2018 survey, 59% of solo practitioners had no conflict software. That number is dated, so check current practice guidance for your state.

faq.question: Can I run conflict checks in Outlook or Gmail?
faq.answer: You can search email for names, but the NC Bar says Outlook and Gmail are inadequate for conflict checking without significant customization. Use email search to find mentions. Keep the official record in a shared list with dates and prior names.

faq.question: What do I do if I already heard details from a prospect?
faq.answer: ABA Formal Opinion 510 says to limit the details you take in and stop the inquiry once you have a basis to decline. Warn the prospect that you have not agreed to act. Then document what you heard and who heard it. Ask your ethics counsel about next steps.

faq.question: Does Lazur check conflicts for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It can explain a screen, point at a field, dictate text at the cursor, and draft a warning email for you to review and send. The conflict search itself stays with you.

faq.question: Does Lazur store the client information I look at?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's client-data rules still apply, so check policy before you use it on a client file.

faq.question: Is there a native Mac conflict-check app?
faq.answer: I could not verify one. The vendors I reviewed are browser-based, and their pages do not name macOS. Check each vendor's own site for system requirements, and test any trial on the Mac you will use.

costs.title: Lost hours on admin work
costs.text: In a Rev and Centiment survey of 550 legal professionals, 49% spent seven or more hours a week on administrative or non-specialized work. Each new prospect adds another search, another pull of old files, and another wait. The hours add up faster than most firms track.

costs.title: Prospects who call the next firm
costs.text: A slow yes loses people. A prospect with an urgent problem will not wait a week for a consultation date. No published figure measures this loss for small firms, so measure your own. Track how many prospects go quiet between the first call and the consultation.

costs.title: Malpractice and disqualification risk
costs.text: Insurance Journal reported that seven of nine insurers surveyed cited conflicts as a first or second leading cause of claims. ABA Formal Opinion 510 also warns that over-collected details can be imputed to the whole firm. A rushed check raises that risk, and a clean record lowers it.

causes.title: Checks run from memory
causes.text: The NC Bar describes solo and small-firm checks that rely on recall. Someone asks the room, or circulates a paper form, and trusts what people remember. These checks happen in the moment. When the person who remembers is out, the check stalls or gets skipped.

causes.title: Name variants slip through
causes.text: Misspellings, similar-sounding names, maiden names, aliases, and former entity or d/b/a names all hide conflicts from an exact-match search. The NC Bar recommends fuzzy searching and recording prior names. Without both, each prospect triggers a manual hunt through old files.

causes.title: Related parties are not recorded
causes.text: Witnesses and the principals of an entity often never make it into the record. When a prospect mentions a business partner or a surveyor, the check cannot find a name it never stored. The gap shows up later, after the work has begun.

causes.title: Tools that were not built for it
causes.text: The NC Bar says spreadsheets, Outlook, and Gmail are inadequate for conflict checking without significant customization. Duplicate entry adds time too. The same name gets typed into the intake form, the sheet, and the calendar. Each copy is a place for a mismatch.

causes.title: Checks that happen too late
causes.text: When the check runs after the consultation, the details are already on the table. ABA Formal Opinion 510 says to stop inquiry once there is a basis to decline. A late check means the inquiry has already gone too far. Rechecks also get skipped when a new party joins mid-matter.

fixes.title: Gather names before the consultation
fixes.text: Build a standard intake form in Word with fields for the caller, the adverse party, prior names, spouses or former spouses, related companies, and witnesses. Use File > Save As to store it as a template. Open it from the template for every new prospect. A form makes the names visible before anyone speaks about the case.

fixes.title: Search the variants every time
fixes.text: Search each name as given, as a likely misspelling, and with any former or maiden name. Record the variants you searched, so the next search repeats the work correctly. If your tool lacks fuzzy matching, run the variants by hand. Log the date and the names in the record.

fixes.title: Keep one shared list with dates
fixes.text: Use one list that everyone reads and updates. Add columns for matter, names searched, date checked, and checked by. A dated log shows what was cleared and when. It also tells you what to re-run when a party changes.

fixes.title: Re-run when parties change
fixes.text: The NC Bar says to check again before providing legal services, when a new party joins, and when a lawyer with prior experience is hired. Create a reminder for each trigger. In Apple Reminders, add a due date, the matter name, and the names to search in the note.

fixes.title: Warn the prospect and stop early
fixes.text: ABA Formal Opinion 510 says to tell the prospect you have not agreed to take the matter. Stop asking for details once you have a basis to decline. A short written line works. Say you have not agreed to act, and ask the prospect to hold details until you confirm.

fixes.title: Screen laterals before the offer
fixes.text: Run conflicts for a lateral's prior matters before the offer goes out. The ABA Journal notes these checks usually happen before a formal hire. ABA Formal Opinion 09-455 covers sharing basic conflicts information with careful timing and need-to-know limits.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write the intake form
plan.text: Open Word and build one intake template. Add fields for the caller, the adverse party, prior names, related companies, and witnesses. Save it with File > Save As. Share the template with everyone who takes intake calls.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Start the shared list
plan.text: Create one list for every matter checked. Add columns for names searched, date checked, and who checked. Enter the matters open this week so you have a baseline to compare against.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Add name variants
plan.text: For each name on the new form, write the variants you will search. Include misspellings, maiden names, and former entity names. Put the variants in the list so the next search repeats the work.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set re-run reminders
plan.text: In Apple Reminders, create a reminder for each trigger the NC Bar names. Include new parties, pre-engagement checks, and lateral hires. Put the matter name and the names to search in each note.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Measure and fix one step
plan.text: Review how many days each check took this week. Find the slowest step. Fix only that step next week, then measure again. Small changes are easier to judge than a full rebuild.
